claim: NAS methods must be compared against both random sampling (a single random draw, ~zero runtime) and random search (an anytime procedure that evaluates multiple random samples over the same time/compute budget as the method being compared) as two distinct, non-interchangeable baselines.
stance_target: correct methodology standard for validating a claim that an LLM-guided search 'beats random search'
scope_conditions: General NAS methodology, formalized as Definitions 9 and 10, Best Practice 8
quoted_support: Random search draws random samples from the architecture space, evaluates them (with a criterion to be defined, such as a short training run or the full evaluation pipeline), and keeps track of the incumbent architecture with the best evaluation so far. At any given time, when stopped it returns this incumbent architecture. Random search is an anytime procedure that should be run for the same amount of time as other approaches being compared to.

claim: Because NAS methods are almost always stochastic, papers must perform multiple runs with different, ideally reported/reproducible seeds (e.g., seeds 1 through 10) and report mean and standard deviation (or median and quartiles if noise is asymmetric) rather than a single run.
stance_target: sample-size and seed-reporting standard a NAS-adjacent LLM paper must meet
quoted_support: NAS methods are almost always stochastic. Therefore, re-running the same method on the same dataset does not necessarily lead to the same result... we recommend that, if possible in terms of compute budgets, all methods should be repeated several times with different seeds and the authors should report mean and standard deviation.

claim: Tabular NAS benchmarks (NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-301 as surrogate) let researchers evaluate architectures via table lookup instead of costly retraining, enabling reproducible large-scale comparisons; NAS-Bench-101 was the first such tabular benchmark, covering 423k architectures in a constrained cell space.
stance_target: which evaluation surface (tabular benchmarks) is expected for rigorous NAS claims, matching the query's named benchmarks
scope_conditions: Definitions and Table 1 of the paper, as of Nov 2020
quoted_support: Another prominent NAS benchmark is NAS-Bench-101 (Ying et al., 2019), the first tabular NAS benchmark. On top of a publicly available search space, training pipeline and dataset, it also provides pre-computed evaluations with that training pipeline for all possible cells in the search space.

claim: Many current NAS benchmark search spaces are relatively easy, such that even random search performs within 0.5% of the optimum, meaning claimed improvements over random search must be interpreted against a narrow achievable ceiling.
stance_target: a modest claimed margin of an LLM-guided method over random search may not be practically or statistically meaningful given how strong random search already is on common benchmarks
scope_conditions: Section 5, discussing benchmark difficulty as a desirable diversity property
quoted_support: Many of the current NAS benchmarks are relatively easy in the sense that even random search performs very well (often within 0.5% of optimal), and we would encourage also including some benchmarks where the best architectures perform substantially better than the ones found by random search.
numbers: random search often within 0.5% of optimal on current benchmarks

claim: The evaluation protocol must match between the method and its baseline: sampling a single final architecture is not comparable to sampling and evaluating thousands of architectures to select the best, since the latter is a fundamentally different (much less efficient but stronger) evaluation regime.
stance_target: estimand correctness -- mean-of-population vs expected-best-of-k under a fixed budget must be matched between method and baseline
scope_conditions: Best Practice 6, general NAS evaluation protocol standards
quoted_support: In some cases, the outcome of a NAS run is only taken to be a single final architecture; in other cases, thousands of architectures are sampled and evaluated in order to select the best one. Of course, the latter is much less efficient, but it can lead to better performance. These different evaluation schemes are one of the reasons why results from different NAS papers are often incomparable.

claim: This methodology paper explicitly credits Li and Talwalkar (2019) and Sciuto et al. (2019) among the works that 'led to serious scepticism of outsiders concerning NAS,' establishing these as the load-bearing prior methodological critiques any new NAS paper (including LLM-guided NAS) is expected to engage with.
stance_target: identifying the strongest published methodological critiques of NAS evaluation that a paper in this space would be expected to address
quoted_support: we note that there are several recent papers that cast doubts on much of the work in the field of NAS (Sciuto et al., 2019; Li and Talwalkar, 2019; Xie et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020), and these have led to serious scepticism of outsiders concerning NAS.
entities: Yang et al. 2020 (NAS evaluation is frustratingly hard)
